Surprise: the Jev you all know and love ( jev-1.13.0 ) was multimodal all along! Image support is fully composable via a find-and-replace in assets . You can put them anywhere that our JSON interface supports: in the state , instructions , or even criteria ! As CEO and Managing Partner, Lydia oversees the firm's six offices in Atlantic Canada, more than 250 lawyers, and over 350 staff on any given day. As Chief Strategy and Innovation Officer and Partner, Paul co-chairs the firm's AI and Technology Steering Committee, drives strategy and innovation across the firm, and is now Managing Director of Stewart McKelvey’s newest venture: the Fortified Firm. Eleven years ago, the two of them made the case to the firm's partnership board for something no one at Stewart McKelvey had done before: a dedicated practice innovation function. Its job was to systematically improve how the firm practiced law, covering everything from process and pricing to technology and profitability. They made that call years before generative AI existed, which is largely why the firm was ready to move fast once AI arrived to the business of law in a substantive way. Two different starting points, one shared instinct Lydia's path to leadership ran through in-house roles first. Those years gave her an early look at how good businesses are run, rather than just the legal work layered on top of them. Sitting on the client side meant understanding different law firms' value for herself, and taking on project work that stretched beyond legal advice into the operational side of the business. "They always let me do a little bit more than just the law," she says. "And I enjoyed that quite a bit." She became CEO and Managing Partner in August 2015, and has since been balancing the collegiality of a partnership alongside the discipline of running Atlantic Canada’s largest law firm. Early on, she pushed back when a senior partner insisted the firm was a partnership, not a business, telling him they were "professionals in a big business." This ability to see what's working ‘under the hood’ is what took her from evaluating outside counsel to running a substantial business. Paul came to law with a background in finance and technology. "I just started to look at opportunities to systematize, improve processes, solve problems," he says, recalling his first summer at work. Lydia noticed early. He'd solve the problem, but he'd also build something everyone else at the firm could use." By his fifth or sixth year practicing, Paul took a secondment to work on technology projects, and a trip to a legal conference in Chicago sharpened his sense of urgency. blogs.content: Insights How to Implement and Track a Litigation Hold Across Every Custodian Learn how to implement a litigation hold, track custodian compliance, handle scope changes, and support a defensible preservation process. by Harvey Team • Oct 20, 2026 A litigation hold is easy to treat as a communication task. Identifying the right employees, sending a notice, and collecting responses. The harder work starts after that as custodians change roles, new data sources surface, claims evolve, and the legal team still needs to be able to show what the organization asked people to preserve and how that scope changed over time. To implement a litigation hold effectively, legal teams need a repeatable way to define scope, map custodians to relevant systems, issue matter-specific instructions, document follow-up, resolve exceptions, and release the hold when the preservation obligation ends. The goal isn’t paperwork for its own sake, it’s a record that lets counsel explain what the organization did, when it did it, and why. This article focuses on that full lifecycle. For a deeper look at the notice itself, our previous guide to drafting a matter-specific litigation hold notice covers how to turn the triggering matter and preservation scope into instructions employees can act on. A Litigation Hold is an Ongoing Preservation Process, Not a One-Time Notice A litigation hold is a written directive to preserve potentially relevant information , but the directive sits inside a broader preservation process. In U.S. federal litigation, the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure address the loss of electronically stored information (ESI) that should’ve been preserved in anticipation or conduct of litigation. A useful benchmark is the HHS litigation hold policy , which requires the agency to identify custodians, track confirmations, revise scope, send reminders, document newly discovered information or custodians, and communicate when a hold is lifted. Private organizations use different procedures, but the consistent thread is that preservation has to be managed over time. That’s also why both under-preservation and over-preservation can create problems. A scope that’s too narrow can miss evidence, while a scope that’s too broad can freeze large amounts of data that later have to be collected, processed, and reviewed. Good hold management keeps the scope tied to the matter as it develops. 1. Define What the Litigation Hold Actually Needs to Preserve Start with the facts that triggered the preservation duty, not with the template. Counsel should identify the claims or issues that are reasonably in play, the events they turn on, the relevant time period, and the types of information that could affect those questions. A practical initial scope should answer four questions: What issues matter? Which people are likely to have relevant information? Which systems or repositories may contain it? What date range is reasonably connected to the dispute? Those answers give the hold a working boundary and make the later notice more specific. However, the first scope is not necessarily the final scope. New allegations, interviews, document review, or discovery can surface additional custodians or sources. Treat the initial scope as a reasoned starting point that counsel can revisit instead of a fixed list created on day one. 2. Build a Custodian and Data-Source Map Before Sending the Hold Once the legal team knows what information might matter, the next step is to map who’s likely to control it and where it lives. This is where a generic employee list becomes a matter-specific custodian map. Identify the People Who May Control Relevant Information The obvious custodians are the people directly involved in the events at issue, but the list often extends beyond them. Managers, employees copied on key communications, IT or records personnel, former employees, departing employees, and appropriate third parties may all control information that matters to the case. blogs.content: Insights What Happens to Emails and Side Letters Under an Entire Agreement Clause or Merger Clause? Emails, side letters, and sales promises rarely reach the signed contract. Here's how to find them and test each against the entire agreement or merger clause. by Harvey Team • Oct 19, 2026 Consider a sales email that promises 24-hour support, in a deal whose Order Form never mentions it. Whether that email still counts depends largely on a single paragraph of boilerplate. That paragraph is the entire agreement clause. It states that the signed contract is the parties' complete agreement on its subject matter, and it supersedes the earlier agreements, proposals, representations, and communications it names. US lawyers usually call the same provision a merger clause or an integration clause. This article describes how to find promises like that one in the deal correspondence and test each against the clause, both before signature and after a dispute. Harvey locates the communications and flags the conflicts, and lawyers decide what they mean under the governing law. Drafting the clause itself is a separate subject, and Harvey's guide to drafting clauses in legal documents is a good place to begin. Delivery Dates, Support Levels, and Pricing Terms get Settled in Email Commercial deals rarely live in one document, which is why the commitments are spread across several places by the time the contract is signed: Email threads hold delivery dates the account team confirmed and support levels the technical team promised during diligence. Term sheets and letters of intent settle pricing conditions that often never reach the long-form draft. Side letters address one customer's requirement while the main agreement stays on the provider's standard form. Requests for proposals (RFPs) and sales decks describe functionality, timing, and service levels that the agreement does not convert into warranties or obligations. Reliance on a message does not make it part of the contract. The signed documents either preserve it, supersede it, incorporate it, or leave its effect to the governing law. Finding the 24-hour support email before signature gives the team a chance to decide whether the commitment belongs in the signed contract. One Vault Holds the Emails, Decks, and Side Letters Together Locating that email by hand means searching inboxes, shared drives, and deal folders. A Vault in Harvey holds up to 100,000 files, including email files and their attachments, so the whole deal can be loaded in one place. Some of the correspondence will still sit in an inbox. With full inbox search turned on, Harvey for Outlook lets a lawyer ask a plain-language question about a deal and then Harvey searches the inbox for the answer. The setting is optional and off by default. Once the correspondence is in, a Review Table converts the messages into rows. Each row captures the sender, recipient, subject, and any commitment the message makes. The 24-hour support promise appears as a single row. With Harvey II, an agent begins each step already holding the deal's documents and history, which removes the need to brief it again. blogs.content: Product Improving Agent Accuracy With Harvey Graph Harvey Graph organizes legal and matter data, maps how it connects, and hands that structure to agents at run time so they deliver high quality, personalized work. by Harvey Team • Oct 19, 2026 If you have used an AI tool for legal work, you know the ritual. Before you can ask your question, you explain the situation. You upload the documents. You describe the client, the deal, and how your partner likes things done. Then you ask. And on the next matter, you do it all again. That routine is changing, in part because models have become much better at legal task execution. We benchmark new models on agentic legal work in Harvey LAB, and the results show how far their capabilities have advanced. When every agent can reason well, what separates them for legal use cases is what they know before they start: context about the matter, the documents, the precedents, your client preferences, and the way your team works. That context is where agent quality succeeds or fails. Harvey Graph helps provide that context. It organizes firm data and legal knowledge and maps how they connect, so an agent starts a task the way a well-briefed teammate would: already knowing your preferences, the project, and the precedents that matter to the work. Watch Video Harvey has spent the past year investing in this context layer of our platform. With the release of Harvey II this month, Spaces provide a closed, private graph of your matter’s data, how it fits together, and how it connects to the people who use it. Additionally, our US Case Law knowledge source uses a graph to map citations and relationships across the body of American case law. We refer to the combination of all these specialized graphs, and the graphs we have in development, as Harvey Graph. Users will never have to know the graph is there or activate it. But they will notice Harvey asking less of them up front, while consistently delivering accurate work that is verifiable with citations. How Harvey Graph Improves Agent Answer Quality Legal work goes beyond being able to read and understand the latest case or draft. It’s highly relational, so agents need to be able to navigate those relationships to deliver accurate outputs. A single credit agreement arrives with drafts, amendments, and side letters, and an agent has to know which version controls before it can answer anything about it. A diligence finding depends on a change-of-control clause, the counterparty it names, and the deal timeline it sits in. Lawyers hold these connections in their heads, and without a graph, agents try to rebuild and assume the connections from raw data and files on every task. Flat retrieval (chunks ranked by similarity) finds passages, not relationships. An agent working this way re-discovers the same entities and cross-references task after task, spending time and tokens to recover structure that was already in the documents. The technical solution sounds simple: better-organized context, a graph that maps the relationships between documents, work product, people, matters, and knowledge. The difficulty is in the word “relationships.” A firm’s data doesn’t announce how it connects. Nothing in a document says it’s the fourth draft of an agreement that was later superseded, that the counterparty in it is the same entity under a different name in another matter, or that the case it relies on was overruled last year. All of those connections have to be inferred, verified against the source, and kept current as the firm’s work changes — across millions of documents and governed by existing permissions and ethical walls. blogs.content: Insights Run Your Contract Playbook on Every Draft, Then Refine the Rules A contract playbook only works if it runs on every draft and changes with the results. Here's what Word review flags and when to revise the rules. by Harvey Team • Oct 16, 2026 A contract playbook is the rulebook for one contract type: the positions your team prefers, the fallbacks it will accept, and the point where a deviation goes to a lawyer. In-house legal teams usually own it and apply it to counterparty paper, and some call it a legal playbook. It pays off when the team runs it on every draft and revises it from what those drafts show. Throughout the rest of this article, we'll follow one customer's services agreement, checked against a software company's Playbook, from the first clause to the changes the results send back to the Playbook. Need to pull terms out of hundreds of agreements at once instead? Start with AI contract analysis at scale . Executed Contracts, Old Guidelines, or a Blank Page Can All Seed a Playbook You don't have to start a contract negotiation playbook from a blank table of hypothetical positions. Harvey’s Playbook Builder converts an existing playbook into structured rules, builds rules from contracts that already hold language your team won, or helps you create them from scratch. Executed agreements are especially useful when your written policy and your negotiating history have drifted apart. A good rule carries a preferred position, a fallback, guidance for the reviewer, and an escalation path. Playbook Builder also keeps citations to the source documents behind each rule, so you can check how a standard was built. The hard cases sit between the standard and the fallback. Say your Playbook prefers payment within 30 days and accepts 60. Then "Net 75" lands on your desk. The reviewer needs enough guidance to see why it's out of range and what to do next. You can also mark a rule required, so missing standard language gets flagged. With the rules in place, run them on a live draft. Every Covered Clause Comes Back Acceptable, Needs Review, or Unacceptable Say the incoming draft is a customer's services agreement on the customer's paper. Playbook review in Word checks every covered clause against your rules and shows the result in the draft. Here's how it might come back (illustrative): Clause Incoming language Playbook result Next action Payment terms Net 75 Needs review Fallback allows net 60, so counter at 60 Liability cap Unlimited for data breach Unacceptable Negotiate to the capped position Governing law Delaware Acceptable None Assignment Consent not required for affiliate transfers Needs review Fallback allows affiliate transfers with notice "Acceptable" means the clause fits a position you've already approved. "Needs review" is your queue, and "unacceptable" is your negotiation list. You stay in control either way. After reading Harvey's reasoning, you check the proposed language and accept edits as tracked changes inside Harvey for Word , right where you already draft. No copying clauses into another tool. blogs.content: Insights Regulatory Consent Order Compliance Depends on a Remediation Record That Outlasts the Team A consent order commits you to fixes, deadlines, and proof. Here's how legal maps each paragraph to an owner and keeps the evidence behind it together. by Harvey Team • Oct 16, 2026 A consent order can outlast the team that negotiated it. By the final report, the lawyer filing it may never have met the people who shaped the original terms. A durable remediation record connects the current team to the decisions and evidence that came before it. A regulatory consent order is a binding order, entered with the respondent's consent, that requires specific corrective actions by set deadlines. Depending on the proceeding, a regulator or a court enters it. Duration varies. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC), for example, ordinarily ends its administrative orders in consumer protection and competition matters after 20 years under a 1995 sunset policy (60 Fed. Reg. 42,569). That policy does not cover federal court orders, and other regulators set their own terms. Keeping that record usable for years takes close reading of the order and a clear link from every commitment to its proof. Legal AI can take on much of that reading. Harvey can structure the order paragraph by paragraph, mapping each commitment to its deadline and the evidence the team expects to use to show completion. The work lives in one place, so the next team picks up where the last one stopped. This article follows one order from receipt to closure and shows where Harvey supports the work at each stage. Teams still turning new regulations into policies and controls should start with compliance management. Responding to the original notice of violation and tracking contractual obligations after signature are separate jobs with separate records. Each Operative Paragraph Becomes a Commitment With a Deadline and Proof A long order mixes findings, definitions, recitals, and operative provisions. Findings record what the regulator concluded, and definitions control how the rest of the order reads. Only the operative paragraphs tell the respondent what to do. Harvey breaks dense regulatory text into obligations, deadlines, and the responsible parties the text names , so the team can work from those paragraphs. A Review Table gives that work a shape: one row for each operative commitment, in the order's own words, with its deadline and the evidence expected to show completion. Ambiguous terms go to a review queue, where a lawyer resolves them before anyone builds a task on a guess. A simplified example follows: Order paragraph Commitment Internal owner Deadline Evidence of completion Revise the consumer complaint policy and obtain required approval Update and approve the complaint-handling policy Compliance Date stated in the order Approved policy and board or committee minutes Train covered employees on the revised procedure Complete required training Compliance and Human Resources Date stated in the order Training materials and completion records Submit periodic compliance report Prepare and file the report Legal and Compliance Reporting date in the order Filed report and supporting source documents The order establishes what the respondent owes. The organization decides who carries each commitment out. Harvey helps structure the commitments, and Legal and Compliance assign the owners. Each operative commitment needs at least one plan item, and each plan item should answer a specific paragraph. A plan that traces back to the order is easier to defend. blogs.content: Insights How GCs are Rethinking Legal Work With AI Three in-house leaders share how they’re expanding their teams’ capacity while keeping lawyers’ judgment central to the work. by Harvey Team • Oct 16, 2026 In-house legal teams face a steady stream of work that varies in urgency, complexity, and the judgment required. AI can accelerate first drafts and other preparatory work, giving lawyers more room to focus on decisions that require their deep knowledge of the business. That raises an important question for legal leaders: Which work should the team take on vs. hand off to AI, and where can its lawyers add the most value? At Harvey FORUM in Sydney, Silv Roest, Group Chief Legal, Corporate Affairs, and Sustainability Officer at The Warehouse Group; Andrew Chivers, Regional General Counsel, APAC at Brambles Limited; and Georgette Apostolopoulos, General Counsel at The Star shared what they’re learning as AI becomes part of their teams’ day-to-day work. Their examples offer practical lessons for using AI to change how legal teams work, beyond accelerating individual tasks. Change How the Work is Divided At The Warehouse Group, one of the largest retailing groups in New Zealand, Roest is looking at how a four-lawyer team spends its time. First drafts, summaries, and issue tables are necessary work, but they can make it difficult to reach the questions that need the team’s judgment and knowledge of the business. That makes the division of work a useful place to start. Watch Video Apostolopoulos faced a different capacity challenge at The Star, one of Australia’s leading integrated resort companies. After the legal team downsized, it no longer had an in-house litigator to run an anti-discrimination matter. Her team used AI to help prepare the evidence before asking outside firms for quotes. By preparing the evidence in-house, the team could ask firms to price the work that remained, giving it a way to manage outside counsel costs. Watch Video Both examples start by breaking work into its component steps. Legal leaders can then identify what AI can help prepare, where their lawyers need to apply judgment, and when outside counsel’s expertise is needed. That gives a lean team a clearer way to allocate its time and scope external work. Make Existing Knowledge Easier to Use For a legal team supporting a global business, even a familiar question can take time to answer when the relevant guidance sits across different policies and jurisdictions. Global supply chain logistics company Brambles has 24 lawyers working across 60 countries. Chivers described how his team brought its policies together in an agent that people can query, reducing the need to search through documents each time a question comes in. Watch Video The example offers a useful starting point for teams with knowledge spread across many documents: look for questions that come up repeatedly and require lawyers to consult the same sources. Making those sources easier to use can help the team respond more quickly, while lawyers still assess how the guidance applies to the particular situation. Help Lawyers Evaluate AI Output Making information easier to access also changes the skills lawyers need to practice. Chivers noted that junior lawyers may be comfortable using AI while still developing the legal knowledge needed to challenge its answers. Familiarity with the tool is useful; the ability to spot a missing fact, weak inference, or incorrect conclusion takes training. Watch Video That training can happen in the course of real work. When reviewing an AI-assisted draft, a supervising lawyer can ask a junior colleague what they checked, where the answer came from, and why they agree with it. The discussion helps the junior lawyer develop judgment alongside their ability to use the tool. blogs.content: KI im Rechtsbereich: Was Teams heute brauchen | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Resources Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Perspectives KI im Rechtsbereich: Was Teams heute brauchen KI im Rechtsbereich: Was Teams heute brauchen Category Perspectives published Oct 13, 2026 author Janusch Krasberg Anfang 2026 arbeiteten rund 3.000 Juristinnen und Juristen in Deutschland mit Legora. Bei der Eröffnung des Münchner Büros Ende September waren es bereits mehr als 13.000. Besonders stark wächst die Nutzung in Rechtsabteilungen: Dort hat sich die Zahl der Nutzenden seit Januar verachtfacht. Deutschland hat den Ruf, neue Technologien eher zögerlich aufzugreifen. Bei KI zeichnet sich ein anderes Bild ab: Kanzleien und Rechtsabteilungen setzen die Technologie mit bemerkenswertem Tempo ein. Für den deutschen Markt reicht es nicht, KI ins Deutsche zu übersetzen. Sie muss auf das deutsche Recht und die Arbeitsweise juristischer Teams ausgerichtet sein. In unseren Gesprächen mit Kanzleien und Rechtsabteilungen in Deutschland, Österreich und der Schweiz verändern sich die Fragen. In ersten Tests von KI-Lösungen für den Rechtsbereich ging es vor allem darum, wie verlässlich KI bei Recherche, Analyse und Entwürfen unterstützt. Inzwischen beschäftigen sich die Teams zunehmend mit der Auswahl eines passenden Anbieters, der Einführung im Team und der Einbindung in bestehende Arbeitsabläufe. Bei der Auswahl einer passenden Lösung zeigt sich in intensiven Pilotphasen, wie gut sie zum eigenen Arbeitsalltag passt. Teams bringen dafür ihre vorhandenen Unterlagen, ihr Wissen und ihre internen Vorgaben ein. Entscheidend ist, wie gut Legora diese Informationen nutzbar macht und sich an die Arbeitsweise des jeweiligen Teams anpasst: wie Ergebnisse aufbereitet werden, wie sie in die weitere Beratung einfließen und wie Kolleginnen und Kollegen damit zusammenarbeiten. Was deutsche juristische Arbeit von KI verlangt Wer Rechts-KI in Deutschland einführt, trifft auf konkrete fachliche Anforderungen. Das beginnt bei der Sprache. Eine juristische Stellungnahme auf Deutsch muss Fachbegriffe präzise verwenden, die relevante Fragestellung erfassen und eine nachvollziehbare Argumentation enthalten. Bei grenzüberschreitenden Mandaten kommen unterschiedliche Arbeitssprachen hinzu. Ein englischsprachiger Vertrag kann die Grundlage für eine deutsche Stellungnahme bilden, die anschließend mit einem internationalen Team abgestimmt wird. Eigene Vertragsmuster und frühere Stellungnahmen ermöglichen es Teams, Entwürfe in Legora an den fachlichen und sprachlichen Standards ihrer Organisation auszurichten. Ebenso entscheidend sind die Rechtsquellen. Gesetze, Rechtsprechung und Kommentarliteratur bilden zusammen mit dem Wissen der jeweiligen Organisation die Grundlage juristischer Arbeit. Für KI-Anwendungen bedeutet das: Der Zugang zu relevanten Inhalten, erkennbare Fundstellen und die Möglichkeit zur Überprüfung müssen im Arbeitsablauf mitgedacht werden. Deutsche Fachverlage spielen deshalb auch bei der Entwicklung von Rechts-KI eine wichtige Rolle. Wer Module von Otto Schmidt abonniert hat, kann diese direkt in Legora nutzen. Hinzu kommt der Umgang mit Daten. Kanzleien und Unternehmen benötigen konkrete Antworten darauf, wo Informationen verarbeitet werden, wer darauf zugreifen kann und wie ihre Verwendung geregelt ist. Datensouveränität und Vertraulichkeit gehören damit an den Anfang der Einführung. Wer Rechts-KI für Deutschland auswählt, sollte ihre Qualität an deutscher juristischer Arbeit messen. Gute Ergebnisse im britischen oder US-amerikanischen Rechtskontext lassen sich nicht ohne Weiteres übertragen. blogs.content: Product Making Harvey the Orchestration Layer for Legal Work Legal Work Orchestration brings the phases, tasks, and reviews of a matter or project into the same place as the documents and the agents. by Harvey Team • Oct 15, 2026 Today, we’re launching Legal Work Orchestration , a new way to organize and manage legal matters in Harvey. It connects the phases, tasks, people, and review points within a matter so that agents can execute defined tasks, lawyers can review their work at designated gates, and everyone involved can see what needs to happen next. Watch Video Much of legal work follows a repeatable process. An M&A transaction, for example, moves through familiar phases, tasks, and review points. But the process itself often has to be reconstructed for every new matter from a checklist, a previous deal, or the knowledge of the people who have done it before. AI agents can already complete many individual steps within that process. What they often lack is the structure around the task: where it fits in the matter, which documents and instructions apply, who should review the output, and what happens next. Lawyers still have to provide that context, move the work between people and systems, and track its progress. Legal Work Orchestration brings that structure into Harvey, allowing lawyers and agents to work through a matter together in one place. How Legal Orchestration Works The same structure can support any matter or project a team runs more than once, from an M&A transaction to a quarterly compliance review. Legal Work Orchestration captures that process in a reusable template, carries the relevant context into each task, and coordinates reviews and next steps. Capture the Process in a Reusable Template Templates capture how your organization runs a recurring type of work. When an associate opens a new buy-side acquisition, the Space can already contain the relevant phases, tasks, playbooks, agents, collaborators, and review gates. Innovation and knowledge teams can define that structure once, helping teams follow a consistent process across matters without rebuilding it from scratch. Give Every Task the Context it Needs Each task includes its scope, inputs, and reviewer. An agent assigned a change-of-control review can therefore analyze the relevant contracts and produce a consent matrix without the lawyer having to assemble a new prompt and briefing for that step. Tasks can also be assigned to another lawyer or shared with the client while retaining the relevant matter context. The work no longer depends on one person manually carrying information from one step to the next. Keep Reviews and Next Steps Moving When the agent completes the review, Harvey notifies the designated partner that the consent matrix is ready. Once the partner approves it, the task is completed and the next step can begin. Updates can also be made from email. A lawyer can ask Harvey in a reply to close a task or begin the next one, while the Space maintains a current view of the matter’s progress. Partners can see where the work stands without asking an associate to reconstruct the status from email and separate checklists. The Future of Legal Work Orchestration Before the release of Harvey II in August, every step delegated to Harvey required a lawyer to gather the documents, write the instructions, and move the output to wherever it needed to go next. Legal Work Orchestration reduces that overhead by giving each task its inputs, instructions, and reviewer in advance. Today, lawyers still actively prompt the majority of steps in a legal workflow. We expect that balance to change rapidly. Over the next six months, we expect agents to take on an additional 20% of workflow steps. Within a year, we expect that share to triple. blogs.content: Insights Building a Frontier In-House Organization How legal teams are transforming their departments with Harvey to better serve the enterprise and help the business move faster. by Matt Zerweck and Gabe Pereyra • Oct 13, 2026 Satya Nadella describes the frontier firm as a company built around intelligence on demand, where people and agents work side by side. Inside most companies, the legal department is where that shift arrives first. For the general counsels we work with, the question used to be how to get lawyers to use AI. Now it’s how to run the department on it. Behind that shift are four challenges we hear from in-house teams: Legal as the bottleneck. Lawyers spend too much time on work that doesn’t need legal judgment, instead of working at the top of their license. Rising volume, flat headcount. Demand for Legal grows with the business but headcount and budgets do not. Reactive instead of proactive. Regulatory change and contract risk surface late, when they’re already problems. No portfolio visibility. Contract history, obligations, and outside matters are scattered across systems, inboxes, and law firms. None of these problems stay in one lane. A single contract can be a bottleneck, a capacity problem, and a visibility gap at once. And when requests queue up and the business can’t see where they stand, employees bypass Legal and take legal questions to general-purpose AI tools, outside Legal’s controls. Banning that doesn't work. The frontier move is to give the business a better place to ask, with Legal in control of the answers. The Platform for a Frontier Legal Department Figure 1. The legal department of a frontier firm with everything in one place. We’re building Harvey as one platform for the business, its legal team, and outside counsel. It connects every request, contract, and matter with the documents, conversations, and context behind it. That knowledge, including the department’s policies, prior decisions, and outcomes, is codified in one legal brain that people and agents draw on as they work. Legal decides what agents can handle and where people should make the call. Legal puts that knowledge to work across requests, contracts, and matters. It sets what agents can handle, where people make the call, and when to involve outside counsel. Past matters, outcomes, and invoice data help Legal choose the right firm for the work. Requests come in and follow-up questions, updates, and completed work go back through the channels the business already uses. Each outcome adds to the department’s knowledge, informing the next decision. Figure 2. The platform architecture. Connected systems feed a shared model of the department’s work, with source permissions preserved. Harvey’s products and agents draw on that same model. If a sales lead asks whether a customer deal can include a new AI-use clause, Harvey can pull up the original request, the department’s position on AI clauses, the terms the company has agreed to before, and the EU rules that apply, all in one answer. We've built that connectivity with partners over several years. Harvey runs on Microsoft Azure and works inside Microsoft 365 , from Word to Copilot Cowork. It connects to LexisNexis for primary law, to Docusign and Ironclad for contract workflows, and through the Connector Library to the rest of the systems the department already uses. Resolve Requests Wherever the Business Works Intake extends the department’s legal front door across email, chat, and business systems, including Outlook, Gmail, Slack, Teams, Jira, ServiceNow, and Salesforce. blogs.content: Insights Vendor Contract Management Starts With Legal Setting the Standard Procurement owns the supplier relationship. Legal owns whether the terms hold. Here's how legal sets the standard once and reviews only the exceptions. by Harvey Team • Oct 9, 2026 Vendor contract management is the process of creating, negotiating, and monitoring supplier agreements, also called vendor contracts, so the organization gets the value it pays for while managing risk. In most organizations, Procurement owns the supplier relationship, spend management, and renewal timelines, and Legal owns whether the terms survive a regulator, an incident, or an audit. Those responsibilities are distinct, but they intersect every time a supplier agreement enters the review process. That overlap explains a common problem: agreements reach Legal too late, with key terms already negotiated, or too early, requiring attorney time for matters Procurement could have handled. As contract volume grows, neither pattern scales. A more scalable approach starts by separating routine reviews from true exceptions. With Harvey, Legal encodes its positions once in a Playbook, the business runs a first pass against that standard, and only agreements that fall outside approved positions escalate to counsel. This article covers review and escalation before signature, and it answers one question: which supplier agreements Legal reviews and which the business runs itself. Building the playbook and benchmarking incoming paper against it clause by clause are separate jobs. To see how teams use Spaces for collaboration beyond supplier review, start with Harvey's guide to legal collaboration . Commitments that arise after signature are a different job again: contract obligation management. What Legal Reviews in a Supplier Agreement Every supplier agreement contains two kinds of provisions: commercial terms and risk allocation. Procurement evaluates and negotiates the commercial side, such as pricing, service levels, delivery schedules, usage rights, and commercial commitments. These matters determine whether a supplier relationship makes business sense. Legal focuses on the second kind. Vendor contract review, sometimes called third-party contract review, covers the risk-allocation provisions that need legal judgment beyond Procurement's commercial read: Data processing terms Breach notification windows Subcontractor disclosure requirements Audit rights Indemnity obligations Termination rights Flow-down obligations Regulatory compliance commitments These clauses determine how responsibility is shared when something goes wrong and whether the organization can meet its own obligations to regulators, customers, and business partners. The security stakes are measurable: SecurityScorecard's 2025 Global Third-Party Breach Report found that 35.5% of breaches in 2024 were third-party related. None of this replaces the contract lifecycle management (CLM) system already in use. The CLM remains the system of record for routing, approvals, execution, and storage. Harvey's integration with Icertis works inside that process: users extract terms, analyze them against Playbooks, and determine the level of risk and review required without leaving the CLM. The distinction becomes clearer when different functions look at the same agreement: Function The question it answers Procurement Should we buy from this supplier, at what price, on what terms? Third-party risk management Can this supplier be relied on operationally and financially? Legal contract review Do the terms hold up against a regulator, an incident, or an audit? Each function reads the same document against a different standard. Legal's attention narrows to the provisions that create regulatory, contractual, or compliance exposure, and that's where the reading gets hardest. blogs.content: 60% of SEC-Filed Contracts Contain Errors | Spellbook Labs spellbook.legal cookie bridge --> Overview Findings at a Glance Issues by Company Issues by Founding Decade Issues by Industry Issues by Contract Type Issues by Filing Year Conclusion Methodology and Scope Humans Hallucinate Too Humans Hallucinate Too. 60% of SEC-Filed Contracts Contain Errors Spellbook Labs analyzed 60,000 pages of public-company agreements across 520 organizations. Sixty percent of contracts had drafting errors. When a self-driving car crashes, it makes the news. The scrutiny is warranted, but the headlines obscure the baseline. Human drivers cause far more crashes . They happen every day, yet almost none become media stories. In legal work, AI hallucinations also get the headlines. An AI-generated legal brief citing non-existent case studies. A judge who used AI to create a restraining order and misquoted state law. These are real issues that deserve attention. But Spellbook sees a different side to AI’s impact on legal and contract workflow. We see the human mistakes that are made when volume and complexity are met with limited hours and manual review. In fact, our data shows saved hours, greater accuracy and increased output when AI is deployed. So we decided to dig into the data to prove what we already know intuitively—humans make mistakes too. Using Spellbook Reviews, we analyzed 3,000+ SEC-filed contracts from over 500 companies, spanning 22 years. These were executed agreements from some of the largest and most heavily lawyered companies in the world. The findings showed plenty of interesting trends and fun examples. Six in ten contracts contained drafting issues. Many were minor. But one in 40 was high-risk—defined as changing the meaning of an agreement in a substantially negative way for at least one party—and they were concentrated in provisions that decide who gets paid, who carries the liability, and what happens in a dispute. None of this is a matter of carelessness by lawyers so much as a consequence of the length, complexity, and disjointed nature of how these types of SEC-filed agreements are prepared and negotiated. In this context, mistakes are inevitable. But they don’t have to be. Every company, public or private, will eventually run its contracts through products like Spellbook that will not only spot errors and risks immediately but suggest fixes based on a company’s own agreement context and real-time market data. Issue Example: A loan cap written two different ways. A mining company's loan agreement set its borrowing limit at "One Million Five-Hundred Sixty Thousand Dollars," then printed the figure beside it as $1,750,000.00. The words and the number differ by $190,000, and the mismatch appears twice. If the borrower and lender ever disagree, the contract gives a court no clear answer, and $190,000 turns on who wins. Findings at a Glance This study should be treated as a proxy for how much humans miss. We kept our analysis deliberately narrow, counting only objective drafting mistakes we could verify from the document itself. We could not judge whether an agreement was signed out of policy, drifted off market, or if a company gave away more than it should, let alone what sits inside the millions of private contracts. These numbers should be thought of as the floor, not a full account of everything worth fixing in an agreement. blogs.content: Insights Contract Obligation Management Has to Follow the Contract as it Changes See how legal teams read renewal dates, notice periods, and covenants out of signed agreements so the obligation register matches the contract. by Harvey Team • Oct 8, 2026 A supply agreement required 90 days' written notice before renewal if either party intended not to renew. The obligation register recorded the renewal date, but not the obligation inside the clause: the notice period began 90 days earlier. By the time the renewal date arrived, the opportunity to act had already passed. Contract obligation management is the work of tracking what a signed agreement requires of each party, when each requirement comes due, and what triggers it. The trouble starts when a register records someone's summary of a clause, the way that supply agreement's register recorded only the renewal date. Harvey reads the executed contract and identifies what is owed, what triggers the obligation, and what conditions affect it, so the register reflects what the clause requires. This article covers what happens after signature, and it focuses on reading obligations rather than storing contracts. If you're looking for where agreements live and move, start with contract lifecycle management . For the wider in-house process around them, see in-house contract management . Three adjacent disciplines get discussed together even though they answer different questions: Discipline The question it answers Contract lifecycle management Where is the agreement, and what stage is it in? Contract obligation management What did we commit to, and when does it come due? Regulatory obligation mapping What do the rules require of us, independent of any contract? Why the Obligation Register Goes Stale World Commerce & Contracting's August 2025 study found an average value erosion of 8.6% from poor contract management. An obligation register is often populated once, when the agreement is signed, based on the understanding of the person reviewing the contract at that point. From then on, the register stays static while the contract continues to evolve, and three gaps begin to emerge: Reviewers frequently summarize obligations rather than analyzing them in detail. A reviewer may record a renewal date without capturing the notice requirement that comes before it. Obligations are often event-driven rather than calendar-driven. An obligation may depend on a business event, a regulatory filing, a financial threshold, or another condition that triggers action only when circumstances change. Amendments alter the underlying agreement. New language can modify deadlines, add reporting requirements, or change existing commitments. If nobody analyzes those amendments and reflects them in the obligation register, the register quickly becomes outdated. Covenant tracking in credit agreements shows how the three gaps compound. A lender may require financial statements within a set number of days after quarter-end, compliance certificates tied to those statements, and notice obligations triggered by material events. None of those commitments exists in isolation, since each depends on timing, definitions, and relationships elsewhere in the agreement. A summary misses the dependencies, an event-driven notice never reaches a calendar, and one amended definition can move all three. Each gap traces back to a one-time reading at intake. Harvey II lets agents inherit the context of the matter or project they open in. For an in-house deal, that includes the counterparty, whose paper the team is on, and the positions the team has taken before. An agent working an amendment starts from that context, so the reading carries forward with the contract. What Reading an Obligation Produces An obligation isn't a single field. blogs.content: Insights AI Fluency Is Legal Education's New Differentiator by Keith Enright • Oct 8, 2026 The team at Harvey is proud to work with more than 100 law schools globally. As AI transforms the business and practice of law, we see an opportunity and an obligation to help educators prepare the next generation of lawyers. Employers increasingly expect graduates to use AI in practice, while educators rightly insist that students develop independent judgment and analytical skills. These aims belong together: using AI well requires students to question its output, test its limits, and decide when to set it aside. That fluency takes guided practice alongside a rigorous legal education. Working hand in hand with educators, we aim to help students build the skills necessary for today’s and tomorrow's legal industry. The Need for Adaptation is Evident For most of my career, I’ve worked closely with senior legal leaders at the intersection of technology and the delivery of legal work. We’ve talked about the future of the profession, the challenges and opportunities we are facing, and how technology can help lawyers thrive and deliver more client value. There has always been discussion of how the profession must adapt to new technology, but the urgency and prominence of these issues has accelerated noticeably in the last 12 months. This shift has been coupled with a growing recognition of the need for incoming lawyers who can use AI thoughtfully and responsibly from their first day. Many firms are investing heavily in AI and anticipate that digitally native graduates will arrive fluent and excited to use these tools. But that influx of AI-fluent talent is taking longer to deliver than many presumed. Even when first-years show up ready to work in an AI-enabled practice, many are still inexperienced with the leading tools, as they haven’t yet had sufficient experience using them to deliver legal work. In these circumstances, the burden of AI training is increasingly shifted to employers, delaying the ability of young lawyers to deliver value on client work and forcing tenured employees to become trainers. Increasing law student exposure to AI during legal education benefits future associates by making them more marketable to employers of all kinds and more immediately productive. It benefits employers when new hires deliver more value more quickly. And it benefits the schools themselves by strengthening their relationships with potential employers, and giving prospective students more confidence in their post-graduation prospects. AI fluency means something specific here. It means knowing when AI can improve the work, how to prompt effectively and interrogate its output, how to fold it into legal reasoning, where it tends to fail, and when to set it aside entirely. That's a professional skill, and like every professional skill, it takes practice. Students who get reps practicing how to work with AI in school will be able to work more effectively and efficiently when they start their legal careers. The core tension is easy to state. The profession's expectations of a first-year lawyer are changing more rapidly than law schools are adapting their curricula and policies. Navigating the challenges of permitting and enabling the use of AI responsibly during legal education must be aligned with evolving employer requirements and expectations. Judgment and fluency, together I hear a second concern just as often, sometimes in the same conversation. Professors and senior partners worry that young lawyers who lean too heavily on AI won't build the analytical foundation and judgment they'll need to become great lawyers. Both worries are legitimate, and they point to the same growing necessity. Legal education needs to produce lawyers who can think critically and use AI fluently. The two skills reinforce each other. blogs.content: Technical Building Harvey’s MCP Policy Engine Runtime controls add another layer of protection for Harvey and its customers by governing tool access, information flow, and agent actions beyond the initial connector review. by Suha Sabi Hussain , Divya Sudhakar , and Nick Gonella • Oct 7, 2026 Legal teams work across research platforms, document management systems, and communication tools. Connecting Harvey Agents to those systems gives them more context and more ways to help users complete work. It also creates a security challenge: tools can change after initial review, return malicious instructions, or be exploited in ways that expose sensitive information. As we rebuilt our Connector Library , we built a Model Context Protocol (MCP) Policy Engine to govern how agents use partner MCP tools throughout a workflow. Prompt injection remains an open problem in AI security, so our approach draws on security research and uses multiple architectural controls to reduce the likelihood and impact of misuse. Our design draws inspiration from Sondera , Progent , ETDI , and CaMeL , which explore enforcing policies outside the model, limiting tool privileges, and controlling information flow. These ideas inform the boundaries we enforce as agents use partner MCP tools. In this post, we explain how the controls work, what we’ve learned, and where we’re continuing to improve. Why MCP Integrations Need Runtime Controls MCP expands what agents can do through a common, reusable standard for discovering tools, accessing data, and acting across services. It also expands the attack surface: bringing externally supplied tool definitions, content, and interaction requests into an agent’s workflow while also increasing existing supply chain risk. These risks have surfaced in multiple real attack campaigns and disclosed vulnerabilities . Our approach to MCP security starts with four considerations: MCP can grant individual servers power over the workflow. Alongside exposing tools that access data and act across services, servers can, where supported, ask clients to invoke models or collect information from users. This bidirectional design requires explicit limits on what servers can request and what clients will allow. Risk compounds across tools. We are concerned about the “lethal trifecta” : combining access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and external communication can result in impactful prompt injection leading to data exfiltration. MCP makes these capabilities both easy to combine and hard to control across independently evolving integrations. Even a trusted tool can return attacker-controlled content that redirects subsequent calls to retrieve and disclose sensitive information. Security depends on implementation. The NSA describes MCP’s security posture as “uneven and highly dependent on implementation discipline rather than protocol guarantees.” Each server, client, and host must enforce permissions, validate inputs, and handle consent. The protocol keeps evolving. New specifications can close existing gaps while introducing capabilities with novel risks . Our policy engine targets two particularly persistent threats that are harder to mitigate using existing tools. Both can exploit the lethal trifecta to exfiltrate sensitive data. In a tool poisoning attack , malicious instructions embedded in a tool's definition redirect the agent's behavior. In a rug-pull attack, a server introduces malicious changes after it has been approved, exploiting the trust placed in a previously reviewed tool. Security Reviews Start Before the Connection We set and enforce strict security standards for our partner MCP integrations, starting with an in-depth review of each server and its tools. Working with partners, we examine authentication, capabilities, permissions, and data handling; we enforce MCP security best practices and constrain OAuth scopes and tool access according to least privilege where possible. blogs.content: Product Introducing the Motion to Dismiss Workflow, Co-Developed With LexisNexisⓇ Draft a fully researched, citation-backed motion to dismiss in Harvey, grounded in the LexisNexis collection of U.S. case law, statutes, and Shepard's® Citations Service. by Harvey Team • Oct 7, 2026 In June 2025, we announced our strategic alliance with LexisNexis® to integrate LexisNexis AI technology, primary law content, and Shepard's® Citations within the Harvey platform, and to jointly develop advanced legal workflows. Since that announcement, we introduced Ask LexisNexis to bring citation-backed answers grounded in LexisNexis primary law content directly into Harvey. Today, we're introducing the first of our co-developed workflows: a drafting agent for an entire Motion to Dismiss (MTD). From Weeks of Associate Time to a Single Review-and-Approve Loop Drafting a motion to dismiss is one of the most time-intensive tasks in early-stage litigation. Typically, an associate has to read the complaint, spot viable grounds for dismissal, research each ground in the right jurisdiction, check for adverse authority, and draft 20–30 pages of intensely researched arguments. This multi-step process commonly takes 40 to 50+ hours of work. The new MTD workflow streamlines this entire process — just upload the complaint, approve the strategy, review the research brief, and watch Harvey prepare your first draft. How it Works The MTD workflow is agentic: a series of specialized agents plan, research, and draft in a review-and-approve loop, with human checkpoints at the moments where a lawyer's judgment matters most. This loop breaks down into four stages: Harvey reviews the complaint and proposes a set of ranked arguments for dismissal The lawyer approves or adjusts the plan Multiple agents conduct in-depth research on each approved argument A final agent drafts the motion A planning agent reads the complaint and proposes a strategy. Harvey starts by identifying the forum and the governing law, then runs an initial research pass with LexisNexis US primary law to surface up to eight candidate grounds for dismissal. Harvey checks each ground against the specific elements of the claims pleaded — a missing element of a cause of action, a jurisdictional defect, a timeliness issue — while weighing the authority honestly and factoring in choice-of-law issues. Harvey rates each ground by strength, so the lawyer can see at a glance where the complaint is vulnerable and where the motion may be strongest. It then produces a proposed strategy: a ranked set of arguments the lawyer can build the motion around. The lawyer reviews and approves the plan. Each proposed argument is presented with its strength rating and a short explanation of the basis for each rating. From here, the lawyer can approve the plan as-is or give feedback to add or drop arguments before deep research and drafting begin. This is the point in the process where the attorney's judgment has the most influence over the final motion.› Parallel research agents run LexisNexis searches for each approved ground. Agents use jurisdiction-filtered, boolean queries tuned to find cases at the motion-to-dismiss stage. Where state authority is thin, they supplement with federal decisions applying that state's law. This research comes back as a memo for each argument, containing the applicable legal standard and the three to five of the strongest cases. Each case includes a full Bluebook citation, a direct link to the opinion on Lexis+® with Protégé™, its key holding, and how it applies to the specific allegations at issue. The memo also analyzes how the case law supports the theory, including the weaknesses the plaintiff is likely to raise, plus key adverse authority and how to distinguish it. Legal work concentrates on these challenges, providing an ideal stress test for training models to operate in high-stakes professional environments. Legal practice demands an unbroken chain between facts, statutory doctrine, analytical reasoning, and client-ready work product. When given a professional task, an agent must extract core issues from source documents, build defensible arguments, and format its findings to exact task specifications. Simultaneously satisfying all of these constraints is the true benchmark for domain-specific models. We evaluated GLM-Legal across three axes: complex task execution, specialized legal reasoning, and real-world legal workflows. Not just what the output looks like, but what happens around it before anyone trusts it. A coding agent can write code that compiles, runs, and looks clean, and still be wrong in ways that only show up later. Engineers learned not to judge the AI's output alone, but the system built around it: the tests, reviews, and guardrails that catch problems before they ship. There's a name for that system now. Software teams call it the harness, and building it well is harness engineering. What harness engineering is At a high level, an AI agent system can be understood as a model (or set of models), while everything around it is the harness. Writing on Martin Fowler's site, Thoughtworks' Birgitta Böckeler defines the harness as the instructions, tools, context, and checks that decide how the model behaves and how it catches itself when it's wrong. Harness engineering is the process of building and improving everything that defines how the model behaves and how it arrives at a reliable and accurate output. OpenAI's engineering team learned this by building an internal product with no hand-written code . Their takeaway: humans steer, agents execute. Their hardest problems weren’t about the model, they were about the harness. Böckeler organizes the harness into two kinds of controls: guides and sensors . Guides steer the AI before it acts, so it starts in the right place. Sensors check it after, so it can detect its own mistakes before you see them. The human's job isn't just to write clever prompts. blogs.author: Shadi
blogs.description: A conversation with Jerry Levine (Leah), Colin Levy (Malbek) and Rich Robinson (Epiq) Change management is an essential part of getting buy-in and ROI from legal technology investments. The gap between promise and outcome is already showing up in the numbers: legal AI adoption reached 78% in 2026, up from just 23% in 2023, yet […] The post How Much of the Change Management Journey Does the Vendor Own? appeared first on CLOC .
blogs.content: A conversation with Jerry Levine (Leah), Colin Levy (Malbek) and Rich Robinson (Epiq) Change management is an essential part of getting buy-in and ROI from legal technology investments. The gap between promise and outcome is already showing up in the numbers: legal AI adoption reached 78% in 2026 , up from just 23% in 2023, yet actual time savings from these tools have averaged 18.3% against a median vendor projection of 41% , according to research from the Legal Stack. Clearly, more change management is needed to support ROI expectations. But where does “vendor support” end and organizational change management begin? What is it reasonable for buyers to expect from a vendor, and what requires wider, enterprise change? We put the questions to three leaders who sit in different seats – a CLM platform, an e-discovery managed-services provider, and a legal AI company – and let them talk it through. What follows is an edited version of that conversation. No vendor can own transformation on behalf of the customer RICH ROBINSON (Epiq): I think the best vendors help organizations navigate change. What they can’t do is own transformation on behalf of the customer. We can provide the methodology, training, coaching, governance, and measurement. The organization still has to bring the leadership, accountability, and willingness to work differently. In my experience, the implementations that hold up are the ones where both sides share ownership of the journey. JERRY LEVINE (Leah): That’s a useful distinction to draw out, because my role isn’t what Rich just described, and I think buyers often assume every vendor is offering some version of it. Someone in a role like Rich’s delivers a change management program as part of what Epiq delivers. My role is different. I get adoption questions constantly, usually from a GC asking how to get people using the tool. I’ll talk it through with them. What I offer is guidance. You need someone internally, often externally too, who owns that work. COLIN LEVY (Malbek): I’d put myself closer to Jerry on that spectrum than to Rich. Malbek is a software vendor, not a managed-services business. Buyers want a partner now, not just a system. In my experience, that shows up as co-building the product with the customer, and staying in the relationship well past the sale. None of that is change management. It’s what separates a good vendor from one who shows up for the sale and disappears. If neither side has the resources, bring in a third party RICH: That’s why I think it’s important that whoever is running the selection and deployment process goes in with eyes open. You have to be honest about your own resources and about your vendor’s resources. Change management is critical to adoption. If neither side has the acumen or the bandwidth for it, my advice is to hire a third-party implementation partner rather than hope the gap closes on its own. JERRY: That gap is where things fall apart in practice. A customer comes back and asks how to get adoption going, and the honest answer depends on questions that often don’t have consistent answers inside the same organization. What have you done so far? Who’s driving this, and who just signed off on it? If leadership is pushing AI initiatives from the top down without knowing why, those initiatives are going to keep failing, and it won’t be the tool to blame. The “easy button” myth, and its mirror image on the vendor side RICH: I see this from both sides now that I’ve moved to the vendor side. Too many buyers treat these tools as an “easy button.” They’re not thinking about the time it takes to implement and deploy them, and especially the time it takes to get lawyers to change how they work. blogs.content: What's New Week 37 · September 7–11, 2026 Copy page Copy page Test your plugins with claude plugin eval and pop Claude Code Desktop panes out into their own windows. Copy page Copy page Releases v2.1.263 → v2.1.269 2 features · September 7–11 Test plugins with claude plugin eval v2.1.269 claude plugin eval runs your plugin against a suite of test cases, scores the results, and by default runs each case again without the plugin so you can see what it contributes. claude plugin eval init asks you what a good result looks like, then proposes test cases and the checks that score them, tries the suite once, and writes the files. Every run, and every check that has a second model judge the reply, is a real model call on your account. From your plugin’s root directory, have Claude draft the suite: terminal claude plugin eval init When Claude tells you the suite is ready, exit the session that claude plugin eval init opened and run claude plugin eval . to score every case. The summary table prints in your terminal, and report.html under evals/results/ has the per-run detail. Test plugins with evals Pop Desktop panes out into their own windows Desktop In the Claude Code Desktop app, you can pop any pane out into its own window. Drag the diff or terminal to a second screen while Claude keeps working in the main window, then dock the pane back when you’re done. Arrange your workspace Other wins Set maxEffortLevel at the top level or per model under modelSettings to cap the effort level on every provider, including Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud’s Agent Platform, and Microsoft Foundry; any higher level runs at the cap Point --plugin-dir at a folder of plugins to load each immediate subfolder that has a manifest If WebFetch hasn’t finished downloading a page within five minutes, the fetch fails with a deadline error instead of hanging; set CLAUDE_CODE_WEBFETCH_DEADLINE_MS to change the deadline, or to 0 to remove the limit Pass --json to claude plugin install , uninstall , update , enable , or disable to print the result as one JSON object on the last line of stdout When the auto mode classifier blocks an action, the reason Claude receives usually names the rule that matched , such as [Data Exfiltration] When you type / partway through a prompt, you can now pick from a list of matching commands instead of a single suggestion. The list opens as you type in fullscreen rendering. A plugin skill also matches on its name without the plugin prefix In the VS Code extension, click the agent count at the bottom of the prompt box to open the agent map , where you can open a subagent’s read-only transcript or stop it In the VS Code extension, select Hooks or Permissions in the command menu’s Customize section to add or remove hooks and permission rules in your user, project, and local settings Claude can pick a browser-tab icon to match each artifact it publishes In Claude Code on the web, take back a queued message in a cloud session before Claude reads it: remove it from the queue, or press Esc or Up , and the text returns to the message box Full changelog for v2.1.263–v2.1.269 → Was this page helpful? Copy page Copy page Releases v2.1.220 → v2.1.224 3 features · August 3–7 Cross-session messaging v2.1.224 Your Claude Code sessions can now message each other. Claude discovers your other sessions with the ListAgents tool and sends with SendMessage , either when you ask it to or on its own, such as after a change in one session affects what another is working on. A message is text Claude writes for the other session, never your conversation history or files. Available on macOS and Linux. Requires v2.1.224 or later. With two sessions open on the same machine, ask one of them to pass something along: Claude Code Tell the session working on the payments API that users.name is now users.display_name The other session shows a Message from row once Claude has read the message; press Ctrl+O to expand it. To see which sessions Claude can reach, run /list-agents . Message another session Self-hosted environments v2.1.224 Self-hosted environments run Claude Code cloud sessions on your organization’s own infrastructure, in public beta on Team and Enterprise plans. Run claude self-hosted-runner on your machines or containers to turn them into runners. When someone picks your environment while starting a session from claude.ai, the mobile or desktop apps, or claude --cloud , that session runs inside your network, with access to your internal services. An Owner turns on Allow self-hosted environments in admin settings first. Signed in as an Owner, run the guided setup, which walks you through creating the environment and starts a runner: terminal claude self-hosted-runner setup The environment shows Healthy in admin settings once the runner registers. Self-hosted environments quickstart Auto mode becomes the default CLI Starting August 14, auto mode is the default permission mode for new sessions on Pro, Max, and Team plans. If you set a default mode yourself, it stays in place unless you accept the one-time switch prompt, and a default your organization manages doesn’t change. You can still switch modes at any time. Already in effect on those plans: the classifier calls auto mode makes no longer count toward your usage limits. To start every session in auto mode before the switch, set it as your default in your user settings: ~/.claude/settings.json { "permissions" : { "defaultMode" : "auto" } } New sessions then show auto mode on in the status bar. blogs.author: Anthropic
blogs.description: We’re committing a portion of Anthropic’s shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows.
blogs.content: Investing in the public benefit Published Oct 18, 2026 Category Announcements Topics Funding Economic Futures Labor market Nonprofits Leadership See more... Related articles Announcements Jul 22, 2026 A research agenda for the Economic Futures Research Fund View more Today, we’re committing a portion of Anthropic’s shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows. Subject to stockholder approval, 5% of Anthropic’s shares will be committed today, with an additional 2% added at the board’s discretion for every 50% increase in the company’s value above a set baseline. As a public benefit corporation, most of our work in pursuit of our mission takes place inside the company: research relevant to AI safety and interpretability; applied biomedical research; discounts on Claude for nonprofits and scientific institutions. These activities have both a public benefit component and for-profit value, so we house them directly in the company. The Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will have increased flexibility and scale, enabling us to pursue our mission in new ways: for example, we might explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations. One example is labor market impacts. AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers. Anthropic has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing this issue, but given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them. We’re establishing the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund as a wholly-owned LLC—rather than a 501(c)(3) or other format—to give adjustability between different forms of giving. None of the Anthropic equity held by the LLC will be used for lobbying or political giving, in the US or abroad. Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good. It is common practice for tech companies to offer escalating compensation awards to their executives. We are instead directing that equity to the public benefit. This builds on commitments our co-founders and employees have already made. When Anthropic was founded, our co-founders pledged to donate 80% of their equity holdings, and since founding we have also operated an equity donation match program that allows employees to pledge equity which Anthropic matches. Approximately half of our employees participate in this program. When combined with today’s announcement, roughly 20% of Anthropic shares will be dedicated to the public good, plus any additional percentage that could be added if the company reaches specific valuation milestones. In the coming months, we will share more about the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund’s structure and governance, including the valuation milestones that may add to its stake. We will also report on our progress to date against our mission in an upcoming public benefit report.

blogs.description: Earlier this year, we shared an update on our election safeguards. Here, we outline how we’ve continued to strengthen these safeguards ahead of this year’s US midterms.
blogs.content: Chapter 01 : Connecting people to trusted sources Preparing for the 2026 US midterms Published Oct 14, 2026 Category Safeguards Topics Democratic integrity Bias and fairness Safeguards How people use AI Limits on abuse See more... Related articles Safeguards Apr 24, 2026 An update on our election safeguards View more Earlier this year, we shared an update on our election safeguards , which described how we measure and prevent political bias, detect misuse, and direct people to accurate voting information. Below, we outline how we've built on that work and continued to strengthen our election safeguards ahead of this year’s US midterms. How people use Claude for elections and politics Our goal is for Claude to be a useful tool for political conversations, while preventing election-related abuse. That starts with understanding how people actually use Claude in these contexts. To do this, we used Anthropic Insights to develop a new analysis of 250,000 conversations over the course of a recent one-week period. 1 Today, conversations that touch broadly on politics, public policy, or social issues account for about 5.75% of all conversations in the United States on Claude.ai, our consumer app. This includes people turning to Claude to follow the news, conduct academic or professional research on public policy, learn about candidates, and navigate government services. About 0.51% of all conversations are specifically about elections or voting. As we get closer to Election Day, we expect the share of political and election-related queries to increase . This sample suggests people rarely ask Claude whom or what to vote for. These kinds of requests showed up in about 0.01% of US Claude conversations. More often, we observed people asking Claude questions that could help them reach their own conclusions, like where candidates stand on a particular issue. Requests that violated our election integrity policies were even less common, appearing in about 0.002% of conversations. 2 How many US Claude.ai conversations touch on politics, are about elections, or ask Claude whom or what to vote for. Each dot represents 1 in every 10,000 conversations in a random sample of about 250,000 US Claude.ai consumer conversations from September 21 to 27, 2026, which Claude classified using a privacy-preserving method . Because requests for a recommendation on whom or what to vote for are so rare, we show the upper end of a 95% confidence interval for that group. Examples are illustrative only. Most of the requests we see are informational in nature. People turn to Claude to make sense of geopolitical events, research candidates, draft documents, assist with coursework, and weigh arguments for and against policies. What people ask Claude for in political conversations. Conversations were clustered in a privacy-preserving, bottom-up manner through Anthropic Insights . Connecting people to trusted sources Ahead of Election Day, we've added two ways for people to get reliable information directly in their conversations with Claude. As we shared in April, when people ask Claude.ai about voter registration, polling places, or election dates, we’ll continue to display a banner linking to TurboVote, a nonpartisan resource from Democracy Works . Later this month, Claude will start drawing official voting information from Democracy Works into its responses on Claude.ai for users in the US. Someone asking where to vote or what ID to bring to their polling place will now get an answer specific to their state, without leaving the conversation. These responses draw on publicly available information that Democracy Works collects from state and local election sources. Official voting information presented by Democracy Works. Additionally, Claude will begin showing up-to-date results on election night and in the days that follow, so that when people ask for current vote counts or election results, they'll be shown the latest official numbers directly in their conversation.

Related articles Partnerships Jan 27, 2026 Anthropic partners with the UK Government to bring AI assistance to GOV.UK services View more Today, we are expanding our Asia-Pacific operations by opening a new office in Singapore—our fifth in the region—and signing a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the Singapore Ministry of Digital Development and Information. Singapore is one of our most active markets anywhere in the world, and Claude is already powering Singaporean business and government services used by millions of people every day, like GovTech Singapore, Grab, and DBS. Our growing local team will ensure these organizations and many more stay on the frontier with safe, capable AI. “We’re committed to Singapore for the long term,” said Dale Finlay, General Manager of ASEAN at Anthropic. “Our customers here hold AI to an extremely high standard, especially when it comes to reliability and security. Having a team on the ground means we can get even closer to the organizations putting Claude to work on their hardest problems.” Supporting responsible AI in Singapore Kai Fong Chng, Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Digital Development and Information, and Anthropic co-founder Ben Mann signed the MOU on the sidelines of Singapore International Cyber Week. Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo and Michael Sellitto, Anthropic Head of APAC Policy, witnessed the signing. It sets out areas of cooperation in AI safety, security, and model evaluation; research on AI adoption and its impact; and responsible adoption across the public and private sectors. “Singapore has been a leader in responsible AI, with a long track record of investment in model testing and evaluation,” said Mann. “We founded Anthropic on the belief that capability and safety have to go hand in hand. With this MOU, we’ll partner with Singapore to help ensure the transition to powerful AI goes well here, across Asia-Pacific, and around the world.” “Singapore’s approach to AI has always been to enable innovation while keeping pace with its evolving risks. Trust is critical for businesses, workers, and the public to use AI with confidence,” said Chng. “This partnership with Anthropic reflects the Government’s commitment to scaling up the responsible adoption of AI, deepening capabilities in our companies and government agencies, and delivering impact for Singapore.” Our work with Singapore goes back to 2023, when we joined the Generative AI Evaluation Sandbox run by the Infocomm Media Development Authority and the AI Verify Foundation. We later partnered with them on a red-teaming project in English, Mandarin, Malay, and Tamil. Under the MOU, we plan to hold technical exchanges with Singapore’s AI safety, security, and assurance institutions on model evaluation, testing standards, and incident response.
